---
title: "Random assignment"
execute:
  cache: false
---

We continue with the [ManyBabies 1 release introduced on the preceding page](units-of-assignment.qmd). Its design makes a useful distinction between a documented sequence and a documented allocation device. The paper reports four pseudorandom trial sequences, each containing four blocks with two IDS and two ADS trials. The release records the order attached to an infant. It does not document the local algorithm by which every laboratory mapped a particular infant to one of those orders.

```{r}
manybabies <- readRDS("data/manybabies/manybabies1-trials.rds")

stopifnot(
  nrow(manybabies) == 37264L,
  length(unique(manybabies$infant_id)) == 2329L,
  length(unique(manybabies$lab_id)) == 67L
)

order_by_infant <- vapply(
  split(manybabies$counterbalance_order, manybabies$infant_id),
  function(x) {
    observed <- unique(stats::na.omit(x))
    stopifnot(length(observed) == 1L)
    as.integer(observed)
  },
  integer(1)
)

manybabies$assigned_order <- unname(order_by_infant[manybabies$infant_id])

# Construct the infant table in a deterministic grouping order. The two counts
# make the grouping unit explicit even though this page uses only infant age.
infants <- aggregate(
  cbind(
    usable_trials = as.integer(!manybabies$trial_missing),
    metadata_rows = as.integer(manybabies$trial_metadata_observed)
  ) ~ infant_id + lab_id + assigned_order + method + age_months +
    north_american_english,
  data = manybabies,
  FUN = sum
)
stopifnot(length(unique(infants$assigned_order)) == 4L)
```

We can verify the realized order labels and their balance in the release. We cannot use those labels alone to infer the probability rule used locally.

## The assignment mechanism is a probability rule

The [**assignment mechanism**](https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics) specifies the probability with which each [assignment unit](units-of-assignment.qmd) receives each condition. Let $Z_i$ denote infant $i$'s order, and let $Y_i(z)$ denote an outcome the infant would supply under order $z$. Under a verified randomized allocation within laboratory, the assignment-identification link would be

$$
Z_i \mathrel{\perp} \{Y_i(1),\ldots,Y_i(4)\}\mid l(i),
$$

where $l(i)$ is the infant's laboratory. A balanced realized table does not establish this independence. The design record must also specify how order labels were generated, concealed, and assigned.

The release yields the following realized infant counts.

```{r}
order_counts <- as.data.frame(
  table(assigned_order = infants$assigned_order),
  responseName = "infants"
)
order_counts$assigned_order <- as.integer(as.character(order_counts$assigned_order))

knitr::kable(order_counts, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

Orders 1 through 4 contain `r paste(format(order_counts$infants, big.mark = ","), collapse = ", ")` infants, respectively. These counts describe the retained release. They neither prove nor refute a particular random allocation mechanism.

## A relabeling diagnostic

We can still ask whether a measured pre-outcome characteristic is unusually imbalanced relative to a transparent reference operation. Infant age varies sharply by laboratory, so comparing raw order means would mix order balance with the laboratories that contributed each order. We first center age within laboratory. Our statistic is the range of the four resulting order means,

$$
T(Z)=\max_z \overline{A}^{,c}_z-\min_z \overline{A}^{,c}_z,
$$

where $A_i^c=A_i-\overline A_{l(i)}$. We then relabel orders within each laboratory while preserving that laboratory's realized order counts.

```{r}
lab_age_mean <- ave(infants$age_months, infants$lab_id, FUN = mean)
infants$age_centered_in_lab <- infants$age_months - lab_age_mean

allocation_statistic <- function(order) {
  means <- tapply(infants$age_centered_in_lab, order, mean)
  diff(range(means))
}

observed_age_range <- allocation_statistic(infants$assigned_order)
lab_rows <- split(seq_len(nrow(infants)), infants$lab_id)

assignment_seed <- 20261017L
assignment_permutations <- 5000L
set.seed(assignment_seed)

relabelled_age_ranges <- replicate(assignment_permutations, {
  relabelled_order <- infants$assigned_order
  for (rows in lab_rows) {
    relabelled_order[rows] <- sample(relabelled_order[rows], replace = FALSE)
  }
  allocation_statistic(relabelled_order)
})

upper_tail_share <- mean(relabelled_age_ranges >= observed_age_range)

data.frame(
  statistic = "range of order means for lab-centered age",
  observed_months = observed_age_range,
  relabellings = assignment_permutations,
  upper_tail_share = upper_tail_share
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.8
#| fig-height: 3.7
#| fig-alt: "Distribution of the age-balance statistic under within-laboratory order relabeling, with the observed statistic shown by a vertical line."

ggplot2::ggplot(
  data.frame(age_mean_range_months = relabelled_age_ranges),
  ggplot2::aes(x = age_mean_range_months)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey75", color = "white") +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(
    xintercept = observed_age_range,
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Range of order means for lab-centered age (months)",
    y = "Within-laboratory relabelings"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11)
```

The observed range is `r sprintf("%.3f", observed_age_range)` months, and `r sprintf("%.3f", upper_tail_share)` of the `r format(assignment_permutations, big.mark = ",")` relabelings are at least that large. This result is a design diagnostic under the displayed relabeling rule. It is not a randomization $p$-value: the paper does not say that this rule generated the infant-to-order assignments.

## Assignment is not sampling

Assignment governs how conditions are distributed among enrolled units. Sampling governs how infants, laboratories, and stimuli enter the study. Random allocation does not make laboratories or English stimuli probability samples of their respective populations.

The same distinction prevents a second error. Testing method was selected through each laboratory's established practice rather than assigned to infants. Method comparisons are thus observational and laboratory-linked. They should not be treated as if they arose from random assignment.

::: {.callout-note title="Audit the allocation claim"}
1. Which part of the design is directly recorded in the release?
2. What additional record would be needed to verify the assignment mechanism?
3. Why is age centered within laboratory before relabeling orders?
4. Why is the upper-tail share a diagnostic rather than a randomization $p$-value?
:::

Random assignment is a probability rule, not a property inferred from balanced labels. The ManyBabies study documents four order sequences and their realized use, so the evidence supports no stronger claim about the allocation mechanism. We can next use the release to contrast a genuine [within-infant factor](within-participant-designs.qmd) with the between-infant order factor.
